transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-04
Time: 16:00 PST
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Ethan Park (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Iridian CTO), Priya Desai (Iridian SRE), Marcus Lee (Iridian ML Eng)
Links shared: benchmark spreadsheet (https://redwood.apps/bench/iridian), security packet (https://redwood.apps/sec/iridian-soc2), dedicated sizing template (link)

[00:00] Ethan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Ethan from Redwood, with Maya on the technical side. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Liam O'Connor: Liam here.
[00:09] Priya Desai: Priya - SRE.
[00:12] Marcus Lee: Marcus, ML eng.
[00:15] Maya Singh: Maya here.

[02:10] Ethan Park: High-level today we want to understand your latency/throughput goals and run through Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private fit. We're expecting this to inform a pilot/benchmarks.
[02:30] Liam: Right. We're fo— sorry, focus is fraud and realtime risk scoring. User-facing, must be sub-second, ideally p95 around 150-250ms on short prompts, and for longer contextual prompts maybe up to 500ms, not great but acceptable.
[02:55] Priya: We also need streaming for partial responses because some of our UI shows incremental scoring and folks want token-level updates.
[03:12] Marcus: Concurrently we'll have spikes during payroll cycles, so concurrency could go from 10 to 200-ish for a few minutes. Baseline steady concurrency is 30.

[05:00] Maya Singh: Helpful. Can you confirm the average prompt size and model family you plan to use? Are these short structured prompts or long context?
[05:12] Liam: Mostly short: 30-80 tokens. A subset uses 800-1,200 token context for session-level fraud signals. For production we'd likely use an optimized open model — we are evaluating a mid-sized LLM (base-13B equivalent) quantized.

[07:05] Ethan Park: Okay, so two workloads: short low-latency scoring and longer-context inference. For Hosted vs Dedicated: Hosted gives fastest time-to-value but bursty concurrency and p95 guarantees are better on Dedicated with reserved GPU pools. Private (VPC/on-prem) is for the data residency and compliance constraints.
[07:40] Liam: Our security team is inclined to VPC for PCI-scoped flows but might accept Dedicated if we can get network isolation and KMS.

[09:20] Marcus Lee: On token/sec benchmarking, what's Redwood's typical throughput on a 13B quantized model for 1-step generation and streaming? We need realistic token/sec and latency numbers.
[09:32] Maya Singh: In our internal perf profiles, on Dedicated A100 equivalent pools with quantization we see ~450-700 tokens/sec sustained for that class, depending on sequence length and batching. For short prompts the end-to-end p95 can be as low as 80–120ms for single-stream requests when KV cache warm and no heavy batching. With concurrency and batching, tokens/sec scales but p95 shifts.
[10:05] Liam: 80–120ms p95 sounds better than we expected. Is that for single-token responses? We typically output 20–40 tokens per request.
[10:18] Maya Singh: That's for 20–40 token outputs, short prompts. Remember that p95 is sensitive to batching policy — continuous batching helps throughput but increases instant p95 slightly.

[11:10] Priya Desai: Can you explain KV cache and prefix caching? We want to reduce cost for session-based calls.
[11:20] Maya Singh: Sure. We support client-side and server-side KV caching. For sessionized users we can keep prefix/key-value cache so repeated tokens don't recompute. That reduces effective tokens/sec burden and lowers latency for subsequent calls. For Hosted we have shared caching heuristics; on Dedicated you can pin caches to instances for lower variance.

[13:00] Ethan Park: One thing customers like is the smart routing + fallback: if Dedicated pool is saturated we can route to a smaller hosted variant with a heavier quantization to keep latency within SLAs.
[13:20] Liam: How do fallbacks affect consistency of predictions? For fraud, a small shift in outputs could change scoring.
[13:32] Maya Singh: We recommend model variants be evaluated with our eval harness; rollouts can be canaryed and regressions monitored. We'll surface quality deltas in the console. You can also pin critical routes to a single model.

[15:00] Marcus Lee: For benchmarking, what data do you need from us? We have synthetic traces and real anonymized request logs.
[15:10] Maya Singh: The config we need: request QPS distribution, typical prompt sizes, 95th percentile concurrency, and a sample of prompts. Also network topology — whether you'll test from our hosted region or a Private VPC peered environment. We'll run token/sec and latency p95 measurement and share the spreadsheet.

[17:45] Liam: For p95 targets, we're shooting for 200ms across our UI flows at 50 concurrent streams. If that needs Dedicated we want to know cost.
[18:00] Ethan Park: Understood. We'll map cost/sizing—rough numbers show Dedicated reserved nodes for this workload to achieve stable 200ms p95 at 50 concurrency. We'll include burst options.

[19:30] Priya Desai: We need SOC2 and audit logging and SSO with SAML. Also want to enforce RBAC and have KMS integration for keys. Does Redwood support HSM/KMS?
[19:42] Maya Singh: Yes — we integrate with common KMS providers and can accommodate HSM-backed keys for Private deployments. Our hosted offering supports customer-managed keys for an additional control plane. RBAC and SAML SSO are supported via the Console. We'll share the security packet.

[21:05] Marcus Lee: On streaming: If we stream partial tokens to the UI, does Redwood provide event hooks and backpressure? We don't want the UI to flood.
[21:20] Maya Singh: We support streaming over HTTP and websockets with chunked responses. We provide a streaming SDK that supports client-side backpressure and the ability to abort streams mid-generation for cost control.

[23:00] Ethan Park: Regarding benchmarking methodology, we typically run three phases: cold start single-stream latency, warmed KV cache short prompt p95, and burst/concurrency stress test measuring tokens/sec and CPU/GPU utilization. We'll also measure tail latency (p99) and variability.
[23:30] Liam: Can you do a run that mirrors our spike patterns: baseline 30 concurrency ramp to 200 for 2 minutes, repeated every hour?
[23:45] Maya Singh: Yes, we can script that in the benchmark runner. We'll need a traffic trace or at least QPS distribution to set the ramp.

[26:10] Priya Desai: For Private (VPC) deployment, what's the expected operational footprint? Our infra team needs to know if they provide nodes or if Redwood supplies an appliance.
[26:20] Maya Singh: Two options: customer-managed nodes (we provide images + helm charts) or Redwood-managed appliance in your VPC. For on-prem air-gapped we have an installer but that takes longer and needs an on-prem GPU footprint. We'll add a network diagram to the packet.

[28:40] Marcus Lee: Are there known mis-transcription issues with the model names? Heard you have Redwood Dedicated and Redwood Private, any internal names we should watch out for?
[28:50] Ethan Park: Ha, yeah sometimes folks call it 'Redwood Dedicate' in notes. We'll be explicit in our email.

[30:00] Liam: For cost, are we billed per-token for Hosted and an hourly reserved model for Dedicated?
[30:10] Ethan Park: Correct. Hosted is per-token + optional per-request overhead. Dedicated is a commit for reserved capacity, with a hourly rate and overage/burst pricing. We'll put sample numbers in the pricing sheet.

[31:55] Maya Singh: Quick note on quantization: 8-bit and some 4-bit quantization work well on inference runtimes; model architecture affects kernel selection and throughput. We'll recommend a profile after we see your model choice.

[33:10] Marcus Lee: What about determinism? Need identical scoring across replicas for audits.
[33:20] Maya Singh: We can provide deterministic seeds and core pinning; however distributed batching can introduce slight nondeterminism. For strict audit paths we recommend single-replica pinned routes or deterministic-serving configuration.

[35:00] Liam: One more: monitoring. We need per-route latency breakdown and token-level cost attribution.
[35:10] Ethan Park: The Console gives per-route/model dashboards, token-level cost, latency histograms, tracing hooks and error analysis. We'll enable a trial dashboard for you.

[36:55] Priya Desai: On the SOC2 packet, will you include the audit firm and last audit date? We need it for procurement.
[37:05] Maya Singh: Yes, last audit and SSAE 18/SOC2 details will be included.

[38:40] Marcus Lee: Let's talk benchmark targets: can Redwood's dedicated pool hit p95=200ms at 50 concurrent streams for our 20-40 token outputs, with 30-token prompts?
[38:55] Maya Singh: Likely yes with proper dedup and KV cache; we'll verify. If we need stricter p95 (<=150ms) we'd recommend dedicated with lower batch latency and a small burst pool. We'll run the test and report tokens/sec and p95 in the shared spreadsheet.

[41:20] Liam: For the actual benchmark run, can we run it from our VPC peered to Redwood's Dedicated region so network hops are realistic?
[41:30] Maya Singh: Absolutely. We can do a VPC peering test or run from your environment to replicate egress latencies. We'll include both numbers.

[43:05] Ethan Park: Okay, recap of next steps: Ethan will send pricing and sizing; Maya will set up the benchmark and ask for anonymized traces; Liam will provide traffic profile and p95 target confirmation; Redwood to share SOC2/security and dedicated sizing template.
[43:30] Liam: Sounds good. We'll aim to get the traffic profile by Friday.

[45:00] Priya Desai: One last thing: do you have references for payments or fraud customers?
[45:08] Ethan Park: Yes, we can share a short list — will include contacts in the follow-up.

[46:10] Marcus Lee: Thanks everyone.
[46:12] Maya Singh: Thanks, we'll follow up with the benchmark instructions.
[46:20] Ethan Park: Great, we'll send the packet and next steps. Talk soon.

[48:00] Meeting ended.

Notes: Transcript has occasional mis-heard words (e.g., 'dedicate' for 'Dedicated'), and some timestamps approximate. Action items captured above.
